2. Business problem
Suggested time: 65 seconds

SAY IN YOUR OWN WORDS
Imagine a seller serving customers in different countries while storing products in several warehouses. Separate stock sheets and order records can disagree. Staff may promise the same stock twice or struggle to explain a delayed delivery. Demand uncertainty creates both excess stock and shortages. My prototype addresses these problems through linked records, controlled workflows and forecast evidence. I have not measured a commercial cost saving, so I will not claim one.

SHOW / TRANSITION
Connect each problem to a function you will demonstrate later.

IF ASKED
Who benefits? Operations staff need reliable stock and delivery records. Managers need clearly defined reports. Customers need orders the business can fulfil.

4. System architecture
Suggested time: 85 seconds

SAY IN YOUR OWN WORDS
React is the website the user interacts with. It sends requests to FastAPI, which checks identity, applies business rules and uses PostgreSQL to store records. Forecasting runs inside the backend. Redis supports request limiting. Prometheus collects API measurements and Grafana displays them. The database and API exchange data in both directions even though this overview emphasises request flow. Docker Compose runs six local services. A modular backend keeps this laptop demonstration easier to run. The trade-off is that forecasting shares resources with business requests.

SHOW / TRANSITION
Trace one request across the top row, then explain the monitoring branch.

IF ASKED
Why not microservices? Independent scaling can help a larger deployment, but it adds network, deployment and consistency complexity. I would separate a forecasting worker when measured workload justifies it.

6. Inventory rules
Suggested time: 75 seconds

SAY IN YOUR OWN WORDS
On hand is the recorded physical-stock balance. Reserved units are promised to existing orders. Available equals on hand minus reserved. Here, ordering two units changes reserved from zero to two and available from one hundred to ninety-eight. Delivery decreases both on hand and reserved by two. Available stays ninety-eight because the order already reserved those units. Cancellation before dispatch releases reserved units. A stock receipt increases on hand. These example numbers are not the live database totals.

SHOW / TRANSITION
During the demo record the actual starting balance for the allocated product and warehouse.

IF ASKED
Why deduct on hand at delivery? It simplifies this assessment workflow. A production design would distinguish warehouse stock from stock in transit.

7. Order transaction
Suggested time: 80 seconds

SAY IN YOUR OWN WORDS
The API validates the customer and request. It locks the customer before checking the repeat key, then locks candidate stock rows in a consistent order. It chooses one warehouse that can supply all items. Reservation, costs, order, simulated payment, shipment and audit data belong to one transaction. An error rolls back uncommitted changes. If the browser retries a request with the same key and matching details, the API returns the existing order. If the details differ, it rejects the conflict.

SHOW / TRANSITION
Explain idempotency using a lost network response rather than unexplained jargon.

IF ASKED
Two buyers requesting the last item must not both reserve it. Database locking and a check of available stock protect the transaction. PostgreSQL concurrency evidence covers tested duplicate and competing requests.

10. Forecast method
Suggested time: 90 seconds

SAY IN YOUR OWN WORDS
History comes from a separate seeded or imported daily-sales dataset. Eligible series require at least thirty-five observations and recent history. Features include demand one, seven and fourteen days ago, a shifted seven-day mean, weekday and trend. Earlier dates train the model and later dates form the holdout. Predictions proceed recursively without inserting future actual values. A weekly baseline repeats the last training week. The lower mean absolute error chooses the model, which then refits on available history and forecasts tomorrow onward.

SHOW / TRANSITION
Explain that a new operational order changes stock but does not automatically retrain the model.

IF ASKED
The same holdout supports model selection, so it is not an independent final test. Real deployment requires representative data and rolling-origin evaluation. Random Forest is an algorithm. TensorFlow is a framework, not automatically a better model.

11. Forecast evidence
Suggested time: 80 seconds

SAY IN YOUR OWN WORDS
This chart uses the saved test evidence, not invented accuracy. For NT-NOISE-01 / DXB-01, the Random Forest MAE is 1.287 units per day compared with 1.5 for the weekly baseline. Training covers ninety-six days and the holdout covers twenty-four days, from 2026-08-14 to 2026-09-06. MAE means average absolute unit error. RMSE penalises larger errors. This run uses deterministic synthetic data. The current UI evaluation may differ because it has a different run date or dataset. The figures demonstrate evaluation, not proven real-business accuracy.

SHOW / TRANSITION
Point to the units and compare both bars. Do not describe MAE as a percentage accuracy.

IF ASKED
A lower MAE is useful but insufficient alone. Check each series, seasonality, stockout effects and longer-horizon errors. Forecast ranges are illustrative rather than calibrated confidence intervals.

Business analytics shows orders, stock, financial totals and delivery completion. Merchandise value counts goods. Checkout value includes shipping, duty and tax. Technical monitoring measures API traffic, latency and errors. One order can cause several API calls, so request counts cannot be called order counts. P95 is approximately the response duration within which ninety-five percent of measured requests finish. It is not an average. Sparse graphs just after startup may need time to collect measurements.

IF ASKED

14. Security and recovery
Suggested time: 85 seconds

SAY IN YOUR OWN WORDS
Passwords use hashes and the API checks active users, roles and ownership. Transactions protect stock updates. Retry keys help when a response is lost. If the database is unavailable, the application cannot safely accept orders. I would check health and logs, restore service, inspect saved state and only then retry. Backup recovery has been tested into a separate database, preserving the live data. This local deployment uses HTTP, demo credentials and broad staff permissions in places. If Redis fails, the current rate limiter fails open. That preserves availability but temporarily weakens traffic protection.

SHOW / TRANSITION
Explain one failure scenario directly. Keep passwords, tokens and private data off shared source-code screens.

IF ASKED
Production would need TLS, MFA, managed secrets, tighter staff scopes, rate-limit fallback policy, independent security review and tested recovery objectives. Do not claim certification.
